grade_definitions.VERIFIED: Confirmed by primary/archival/government record or by multiple independent reputable sources; safe for verified-only graph edges.
grade_definitions.SUPPORTED: Documented in reputable secondary or institutional source; plausible; visible grade required on graph edges.
grade_definitions.PROVISIONAL: Partial, single-source, or weakly evidenced; treat as lead.

claims.claim: Marjorie Stewart Joyner was born October 24, 1896 in Monterey, Virginia and moved to Chicago in 1912 at age 16 to study cosmetology.
claims.source: BlackPast.org (Marjorie Joyner biography); encyclopedia.com (Joyner biography); National Inventors Hall of Fame (invent.org)
claims.evidence: BlackPast: 'Marjorie Stewart was born October 24, 1896 in Monterey, Virginia... Stewart arrived in Chicago in 1912 when she was only sixteen years old and enrolled in A.B. Molar Beauty School.'
claims.notes: A.B. Molar's first name sometimes rendered 'Moler' (NIHF: 'A.B. Moler Beauty and Culture School').

claims.claim: Marjorie Joyner was the first African American to graduate from Chicago's A.B. Molar Beauty School (1916).
claims.source: BlackPast.org; National Inventors Hall of Fame
claims.evidence: BlackPast: 'Marjorie became the first African American to graduate from the school in 1916.' NIHF: she 'graduated from A.B. Moler Beauty and Culture School in Chicago in 1916.'

claims.claim: After graduating, Joyner opened her own beauty salon on South State Street, Chicago.
claims.evidence: BlackPast: 'After graduation, Joyner opened her own beauty salon on South State Street in Chicago.' SHEEN: 'She then opened her own beauty salon on South State Street.'
claims.notes: Street address not recovered; maps mark approximate location only.

claims.claim: Joyner joined the Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Company and became its national adviser/supervisor for approximately 200 beauty schools (later vice president).
claims.source: BlackPast.org; National Inventors Hall of Fame; SHEEN Magazine
claims.evidence: BlackPast: Joyner 'met Madam C.J. Walker... she became the national adviser to the company, overseeing 200 beauty schools.' NIHF: she 'became vice president of the Madame C.J. Walker Manufacturing Company' and stayed 'for more than 50 years.'
claims.notes: Exact figure (200 schools) approximate; vice-presidency title confirmed by NIHF.

claims.claim: Joyner invented the permanent wave machine and received U.S. Patent No. 1,693,515 in 1928.
claims.source: National Inventors Hall of Fame; Face2Face Africa; patent records
claims.evidence: NIHF: 'Joyner was granted a U.S. patent for her permanent wave machine... U.S. Patent No., 1,693,515' in 1928. Device: 16 rods inside a drying hood to set and straighten hair.
claims.notes: Inventor inducted into NIHF in 2023.

claims.claim: Joyner's wave machine was patented but assigned to (and profits went to) the Walker Company; she saw no personal profit from the invention.
claims.evidence: BlackPast: 'Joyner, however, never saw any profit from the invention, as the Walker Company owned the rights.' ThoughtCo: patent rights 'belonged to the Madam C.J. Walker Company rather than to Joyner herself.'
claims.notes: Wording 'never saw any profit' (BlackPast) is strong; graded SUPPORTED not VERIFIED absent primary assignment documents.

claims.claim: Over her ~50-year career Joyner taught approximately 15,000 stylists.
claims.evidence: ThoughtCo: 'Over her 50-year career, Joyner trained some 15,000 stylists.' Joyner retired from Walker in 1973.
claims.notes: Rounded figure; single secondary lineage.

claims.claim: Joyner helped draft Illinois' first cosmetology licensing laws.
claims.date: DISPUTED: encyclopedia.com says 1924; association-founding context suggests post-1945
claims.evidence: Multiple sources agree on the role. encyclopedia.com: 'In 1924 Joyner helped write Illinois' first cosmetology laws.' Others date it vaguely to her career.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Date conflict (1924 vs. later association period); no primary legislative record consulted.
claims.notes: Needs Illinois session-law verification — priority research lead.

claims.claim: In 1945 Joyner co-founded the United Beauty School Owners and Teachers Association with Mary McLeod Bethune.
claims.evidence: BlackPast: 'In 1945, Joyner and Mary McLeod Bethune founded the United Beauty School Owners and Teachers Association.'
claims.notes: Some sources render the name 'Mary Bethune McLeod'; organization records not consulted.

claims.claim: Joyner organized the first Bud Billiken Parade in Chicago in 1929.
claims.evidence: encyclopedia.com: 'Joyner organized the first Bud Billiken Parade in Chicago in 1929.'

claims.claim: Joyner's salon served a clientele of all races.
claims.evidence: NIHF: her salon 'served clients of all races.'
claims.notes: Single institutional source.

claims.claim: Marjorie Joyner died in Chicago in 1994; sources conflict between December 7 and December 27.
claims.source: encyclopedia.com; Wikipedia; SHEEN Magazine; Face2Face Africa
claims.evidence: encyclopedia.com, Wikipedia, Face2Face: December 27, 1994. SHEEN Magazine: 'December 7, 1994.'
claims.contradictory_evidence: Two different death dates in reputable secondary sources.
claims.notes: Do not assert a single date until a primary record is consulted.

claims.claim: Annie Turnbo Malone founded Poro and established Poro College in St. Louis in 1918.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'In 1918, Malone established Poro College, a cosmetology school and community center in St. Louis.'
claims.notes: Poro operations predate 1918; college date is the firm anchor.

claims.claim: Malone's Poro system created employment for approximately 75,000 women across the Americas, Africa, and the Philippines.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'She is credited with creating jobs for 75,000 women in North and South America, Africa, and the Philippines through her international Poro franchises.'
claims.notes: Figure is company-era promotional lineage; treat as approximate.

claims.claim: Malone moved Poro's Chicago headquarters to 4415 South Parkway ('Poro Block') in 1930.
claims.evidence: ECON-001 notes give the 'Poro Block' address 4415 S. Parkway from 1930; Wikipedia: 'In 1930, she moved most of her business to Chicago, where she purchased an entire city block.'
claims.notes: Needs a stronger direct citation for VERIFIED.

claims.claim: Anthony Overton founded the Overton Hygienic Company in Kansas City in 1898 and moved it to Chicago in 1911.
claims.evidence: BlackPast: Overton 'moved his company to Chicago in 1911.' Racked: Overton Hygienic founded 1898 (per company/narrative sources).

claims.claim: By 1912–1915 Overton Hygienic manufactured 52–62 products, employed ~400 door-to-door salespeople, and received a $1M Dun & Bradstreet rating by 1920.
claims.evidence: Racked: 'By 1912, the company had 52 products, 400 door-to-door salespeople.' BlackPast: '$1 million rating from Dun & Bradstreet in 1920.' '62 products' variant from Racked (1915).
claims.contradictory_evidence: Product count varies 52 vs 62 across sources; sales force number promotional-era.
claims.notes: Approximate period figures.

claims.claim: Overton commissioned the Overton Hygienic Building at 3619–3627 S. State Street in 1922 (architect Z. Erol Smith); it housed cosmetics manufacturing plus other Black enterprises (bank, insurance, offices).
claims.evidence: NPS: the building 'housed cosmetics manufacturing and other Black enterprises'; 'major Black Metropolis business site.' Clio: commissioned 1922; architect Z. Erol Smith.

claims.claim: Overton Hygienic went out of business in the early 1980s.
claims.evidence: BlackPast: 'Overton Hygienic remained in business until the early 1980s.'
claims.notes: Single source; wind-down detail not researched.

claims.claim: George E. Johnson and Joan Henderson Johnson founded Johnson Products Company in Chicago in 1954, starting with a $250 bank loan (working from the couple's South Side home).
claims.evidence: AP: founded 'in 1954 with a $250 loan' (per Reuters/Black Enterprise). BE 2026: 'founded with a $250 bank loan in 1954.'
claims.notes: Johnson had apprenticed at S.B. Fuller's Black-owned cosmetics firm.

claims.claim: Ultra Sheen was marketed to women who straightened their hair as a product that reduced the need for hot combs and frequent beauty-shop visits.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: Ultra Sheen targeted 'women who straightened their hair,' allowing 'less time with hot comb and at the beauty shop.'
claims.notes: Product-marketing positioning; treat as company strategy, not shop-economics proof.

claims.claim: By the 1960s Johnson Products held nearly 80% of the Black hair-care market, with $12.6M sales by 1970, 500 employees and $40M sales by 1976.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (citing sources): 'By 1960, JPC nearly had 80% of the Black hair care market... $12.6 million in sales by 1970... 500 employees and $40 million in sales by 1976.'
claims.notes: Market-share figures are company-era claims; sales growth corroborated by BE.

claims.claim: In 1971 Johnson Products became the first Black-owned company listed on the American Stock Exchange.
claims.evidence: Reuters/AP obituaries (2026-07-07): Johnson Products 'became the first Black-owned company on the American Stock Exchange' in 1971.

claims.claim: Johnson Products was the exclusive sponsor of the television show Soul Train from 1971.
claims.evidence: BE: Johnson Products 'sponsored... Soul Train'; Reuters: 'exclusive sponsorship of Soul Train.' Cross-ref CTL-DR-BMI-002.

claims.claim: Following the Johnsons' divorce, Johnson Products was sold in 1993 for $67 million to IVAX Corporation.
claims.source: Black Enterprise ('Bad Hair Days' retrospective); Black Enterprise (July 2026 obituary)
claims.evidence: BE retrospective: sold 'for $67 million' to IVAX after 'the divorce of George and Joan Johnson.' BE 2026: sold 'for more than $60 million to a pharmaceutical firm' in 1993. Consistent.
claims.notes: Divorce context from BE retrospective; not repeated salaciously in brief.

claims.claim: George E. Johnson died July 6, 2026 at age 99.
claims.evidence: AP/Reuters obituaries published 2026-07-07 report death at 99.

claims.claim: Edward and Bettiann Gardner founded Soft Sheen Products in Chicago in 1964, starting from their basement.
claims.source: The HistoryMakers (biography + oral-history finding aid A1993_004); Black Enterprise
claims.evidence: HistoryMakers: the Gardners 'founded Soft Sheen Products, Inc. from their Chicago basement in 1964.' Grew to 400+ employees; exported to Canada, the Caribbean, West Africa.

claims.claim: Edward Gardner personally delivered Soft Sheen products to South Side salons from his car trunk; Care Free Curl (1981) was sold only through professional cosmetologists, protecting salon revenue.
claims.source: Black Enterprise (Edward Gardner obituary, via Chicago Sun-Times reporting); Black Enterprise (Bettiann Gardner obituary)
claims.evidence: BE obit: Gardner 'personally drove his car... delivering Soft Sheen products... in the trunk of his car' to South Side salons. BE: 'Care-Free Curl was sold only through professional cosmetologists.'
claims.notes: Distribution strategy corroborated across BE obituaries.

claims.claim: Soft Sheen's sales grew from $500,000 (1979) to $55 million (1983); the company ranked No. 8 on the Black Enterprise 100 and was BE Company of the Year (1989).
claims.evidence: BE: sales 'from $500,000 in 1979 to $55 million in 1983'; 'No. 8 on the BE 100'; '1989 BE Company of the Year.'

claims.claim: Soft Sheen was sold to L'Oréal in 1998 (following a 1988 merger with Carson Products).
claims.evidence: HistoryMakers: 'sold the company to L'Oreal in 1998.' BE: 'merged with Carson Products... in 1988 and sold it to L'Oréal in 1998.'

claims.claim: Edward Gardner led a 1983 voter-registration drive for Harold Washington's mayoral campaign that raised $300,000 and registered 200,000–250,000 Black voters.
claims.source: The HistoryMakers (finding aid); news release via TheGrio; Chicago Sun-Times via BE obituary
claims.evidence: HistoryMakers: drive 'registered 250,000 black voters' and raised $300,000. News release (via thegrio): 'helped to register 200,000 black voters.' Sun-Times (via BE): drive registered 250,000.
claims.contradictory_evidence: 200,000 vs. 250,000 across sources; 250,000 figure is Gardner-family/history-maker narrative.
claims.notes: Event is documented; the number is disputed. Use a range.

claims.claim: The National Beauty Culturists' League originated in 1919 and was formally chartered March 30, 1940, as a Black professional organization formed under segregation from white trade groups.
claims.source: NBCL official site; Walker (2008), Journal of Women's History (via excerpt)
claims.evidence: NBCL: 'originated in 1919... chartered March 30, 1940'; mission: standards, legislation, education. Walker 2008: NBCL founded 1919 'in response to segregated beauty trade organizations.'
claims.notes: The segregation-rationale claim is mediated via scholarly excerpt.

claims.claim: Martin Luther King Jr. addressed the National Beauty Culturists' League in 1957.
claims.source: Tiffany Gill, 'Civic Beauty,' Enterprise & Society (via Cambridge abstract); secondary references
claims.evidence: Cambridge abstract page lists the article's scope including MLK's 1957 address to the League.
claims.notes: Mediated; full article not consulted.

claims.claim: Black barbershops became 'democratic social spaces' whose proprietors' financial independence sustained civil-rights politics; 19th-century Black barbers mainly served white clienteles, and licensing/professionalization posed racialized challenges.
claims.source: Quincy T. Mills, Cutting Along the Color Line (UPenn Press, 2013) — via publisher description and WAMU/Kojo Nnamdi Show author interview transcript (2014)
claims.evidence: Publisher: 'Black barbershops... became democratic social spaces... the strong-arm of the struggle.' Kojo interview: 'If barbers don't turn a profit... the shop isn't going to be there tomorrow'; 'commerce, community, culture and congregation.'
claims.notes: Book itself not consulted; Chicago-specific instantiation thinner than national argument.

claims.claim: Black beauty parlors functioned as political 'free spaces' and beauticians as organizers; trade organizations also favored established salon owners over home-shop beauticians.
claims.source: Tiffany Gill, Beauty Shop Politics (UI Press) — via scholarly review (The Free Library); Walker (2008), JWH (via excerpt)
claims.evidence: Review: Gill shows parlors 'served as free spaces... beauticians... political organizers.' Walker 2008 excerpt: NBCL favored commercial salon owners; unlicensed home-shop beauticians reported to inspectors.
claims.notes: Mediated scholarship; books themselves not consulted.

claims.claim: Oscar J. Freeman owned the Metropolitan Barber Shop at 4654 South Parkway, Chicago, and had been in business fourteen years at the time of the 1942 FSA-OWI photograph.
claims.evidence: LOC caption verbatim: 'Mr. Oscar J. Freeman, barber, owns the Metropolitan Barber Shop, 4654 South Parkway, Chicago, Illinois. He has been in business fourteen years.' Rights: no known restrictions.
claims.notes: The only named ordinary Chicago shop-owner recovered in this brief.

claims.claim: FSA-OWI photographers documented Black barbershops on Chicago's South Side and 'Black Belt' in 1941.
claims.evidence: LOC items: 'Negro barber shop. Southside of Chicago, Illinois' (2017788743); 'Barber shop in the Black Belt, Chicago, Illinois' (2017729635). Rights: no known restrictions.

claims.claim: Beauty salons offered rare entrepreneurial opportunities to Black women and served as social centers.
claims.source: National Inventors Hall of Fame; Walker (2008), JWH
claims.evidence: NIHF: salons 'provided rare entrepreneurial opportunities to Black women' and 'served as social centers.' Walker 2008: 'one of the few avenues through which Black women could become entrepreneurs.'
claims.notes: General claim; Chicago instantiation via Joyner.

claims.claim: Harrison's Barber Shop existed on the 63rd Street corridor.
claims.evidence: PLACE-001's ordinary-business list names Harrison's but marks it provisional pending directory work.
claims.notes: Do not assert address; cite PLACE-001.

claims.claim: Johnson Products operated a factory in Nigeria.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: JPC 'opened a factory in Nigeria.'
claims.notes: International-expansion detail; secondary citation not independently checked.

claims.claim: Afro Sheen was marketed with 'Black is beautiful' messaging including the slogan 'soul food for the natural.'
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: Afro Sheen marketed as 'Black is beautiful,' with slogan 'soul food for the natural.'
claims.notes: Advertising-history claim; needs primary ad verification for VERIFIED.

claims.claim: Marjorie Joyner's papers are held at the Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection, Chicago Public Library.
claims.evidence: Single secondary biography states Joyner's papers are at the Harsh Collection.
claims.notes: Verify against CPL catalog before asserting; priority research lead.

claims.claim: The National Beauty Culturists' League's 1940 charter lists purposes including standards, scientific practice, education, legislation, and cooperation.
claims.evidence: NBCL: 'originated in 1919, and was chartered March 30, 1940' with purposes around standards and legislation.
claims.notes: Organization's own account.

claims.claim: Joyner led 195 Black cosmetologists on an educational trip to Paris in 1954.
claims.evidence: encyclopedia.com: 'In 1954, Joyner led 195 black cosmetologists on an educational trip to Paris.'
claims.notes: Single reference source; vivid but uncorroborated.

claims.claim: The Smithsonian Institution exhibited Joyner's permanent wave machine and a reconstruction of her salon in 1987; the machine is in the Smithsonian's collection.
claims.evidence: Face2Face: 'In 1987 the Smithsonian Institution exhibited a replica of her salon... Joyner's original wave machine is currently on display at the Smithsonian.'
claims.notes: NMAH Open Access verification is a publication-time check.

claims.claim: No reliable published figures exist in the sources consulted for the number of Black-owned beauty/barber shops in Chicago by decade, or for shop-level revenues, margins, wages, or survival rates.
claims.source: Negative finding across consulted sources; ECON-001 W3-firms-b notes
claims.evidence: Sibling research explicitly flags named independent Black beauty shops as 'poorly preserved' and directory/Defender work as outstanding.
claims.notes: This is the brief's central documented gap; ECON-001 is the designated vehicle.

claims.claim: No evidence was gathered on chain/franchise competition pressure against Black-owned Chicago shops.
claims.evidence: No sources consulted addressed national salon chains' effects on Black-owned Chicago shops.
claims.notes: Red-team flagged; ECON-001 scope.

claims.claim: Joyner's wave machine predated or enabled later home permanents; its invention followed her teaching Walker the Marcel-wave technique.
claims.evidence: Face2Face: 'After teaching Walker how to do the Marcel wave, she was inspired to improve on the tedious process,' leading to the 1928 machine.
claims.notes: Causal/inspirational narrative from secondary sources; not independently verified.

claims.claim: An IIT Bronzeville history booklet documents a barber shop in the Binga Block (State Street, 47th–48th) and door-to-door sales of Poro Products in the neighborhood.
claims.source: Illinois Institute of Technology, 'The Black Metropolis – Bronzeville' history booklet (PDF)
claims.evidence: Booklet text: Binga Block 'hosted a variety of businesses, including a pharmacy with door-to-door sales of Poro Products' and a 'barber shop.'
claims.notes: Shop unnamed; institutional local-history source.

claims.claim: Soft Sheen's Jheri Curl product Care Free Curl debuted in 1981 and was sold only through professional cosmetologists.
claims.source: Black Enterprise (Edward/Bettiann Gardner obituaries); product histories
claims.evidence: BE obituaries date the Care Free Curl Jheri Curl product to 1981 and report it was 'sold only through professional cosmetologists.'
claims.notes: Debut year from secondary product-history lineage; distribution claim is C28.
